forces: Concert band, arranged by Thomas Knox
performers: United States Marine Band; Col John R. Bourgeois
intro: The United States Marine Band, conducted by John R. Bourgeois, plays Thomas Knox’s concert-band arrangement of Kashchei’s Infernal Dance. The Firebird has the sorcerer and his creatures in her power: every jagged leap is another step they cannot resist.
license: Public domain in the US (US Marine Band recording; composition published 1910)

cues.title: A spell with teeth
cues.text: The Firebird forces Kashchei and his creatures to dance. Their own violence turns against them: the short phrases lurch, strike and start again. This is a fairy-tale rescue with very little gentleness in it.
cues.evidence: The ballet scenario describes the Firebird enchanting Kashchei and his subjects into an infernal dance: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Firebird. Marcel Bowman, The Human Versus the Supernatural, pp. 98–99, discusses the dance’s angular motifs: https://collections.lib.utah.edu/dl_files/6e/34/6e3433faa6efb79c80229fe8373f0a7d3aaeab9c.pdf.
cues.how: About the passage as a whole.

cues.title: Small steps, huge leaps
cues.text: The tune squeezes neighbouring notes together, then jumps across a tritone. Those cramped semitones and ungainly leaps give Kashchei’s dance its crooked gait. Even a phrase that seems ready to sing has something sharp in its mouth.
cues.evidence: Bowman, The Human Versus the Supernatural, pp. 98–99, examples 45a–e, traces the semitone and tritone motifs through rehearsal figures 133–141 and 161 of the ballet score: https://collections.lib.utah.edu/dl_files/6e/34/6e3433faa6efb79c80229fe8373f0a7d3aaeab9c.pdf.
cues.how: About the passage as a whole.

cues.title: Karsavina at the Opéra
cues.text: On 25 June 1910, Tamara Karsavina dances the Firebird at the Paris Opéra. Michel Fokine supplies the choreography for Diaghilev’s Ballets Russes. Stravinsky is twenty-eight; this glittering, dangerous bird carries his name into the Paris theatres.
cues.evidence: The premiere date, theatre, company, choreographer and original Firebird are documented at https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Firebird. Stravinsky’s birth on 17 June 1882 is documented by the Fondation Igor Stravinsky: https://fondation-igor-stravinsky.org/en/composer/biography/.

cues.title: Four descending notes
cues.text: One of Kashchei’s recurring gestures crawls down through four neighbouring notes. It is a tiny scrap of melody, easy to pass from one phrase to another. Alongside the wide leaps, that close-packed descent keeps the dance recognisably his.
cues.evidence: Bowman, The Human Versus the Supernatural, pp. 103–05, examples 49 and 52, identifies the descending four-note chromatic motif at rehearsal figures 141 and 160 of the Infernal Dance. This note describes a recurring motif, not a single entrance: https://collections.lib.utah.edu/dl_files/6e/34/6e3433faa6efb79c80229fe8373f0a7d3aaeab9c.pdf.
cues.how: About the passage as a whole.

cues.title: The name that sticks
cues.text: In his 1962 book with Robert Craft, Stravinsky recalls a stranger addressing him in an American railway dining car as “Mr. Fireberg”. Half a century after the premiere, the bird still gets there before its composer.
cues.evidence: Igor Stravinsky and Robert Craft, Expositions and Developments (1962), passage on The Firebird, quoted in Marcel Bowman, The Human Versus the Supernatural, p. 4: https://collections.lib.utah.edu/dl_files/6e/34/6e3433faa6efb79c80229fe8373f0a7d3aaeab9c.pdf. The recollection does not date the encounter.

composer.born: 17 June 1882, Oranienbaum, near St Petersburg, Russia
composer.epithet: He could make a roomful of dancers lose their footing with one displaced accent, then write a psalm that scarcely moves.
facts: Diaghilev’s Ballets Russes · Ramuz’s travelling theatre · Balanchine · Auden and Kallman
Ballets, operas, symphonies and sacred music; composing and recording into his eighties
composer.background:
In St Petersburg, opera was the family business. Stravinsky’s father, Fyodor, sang bass at the Mariinsky Theatre; Igor heard him on stage and began piano lessons at nine. Born in 1882 at Oranienbaum, he entered St Petersburg University to study law. There he befriended Vladimir Rimsky-Korsakov, whose father heard his first pieces in 1902. Rimsky-Korsakov took him on privately, giving regular lessons from 1905 until his death in 1908. The pupil orchestrated pages of Pan Voyevoda, then had to explain why his teacher had scored them differently.

He married his cousin Catherine Nossenko in 1906; by 1914 they had four children. His E♭ Symphony owed much to Glazunov and Tchaikovsky; Scherzo fantastique and Fireworks showed what he could do with an orchestra in a few minutes. Sergei Diaghilev heard his music in 1909 and gave him some Chopin to orchestrate for Les Sylphides. Then came a whole ballet, The Firebird. Stravinsky handed over the score in sections while Michel Fokine worked out the dances. In his 1936 autobiography he remembered the rehearsals ending with dinner beside Diaghilev and Nijinsky, and good claret.
